analysis: Reviewed the two head-text slices (lines 28100-29713) of fixtures/prompt-contract/v1/production_vectors.json, plus the patch excerpt. The file is a golden-vector test fixture for prompt-contract / prefix-cache chain hashes. It contains no executable code, secrets, keys, endpoints or authorization logic. The visible content is repeated token IDs, a "long_prompt" vector with synthetic 'cache' text, plan fields (prompt_contract_id, prompt_token_count 1025, block_boundaries and chain hashes at 256/512/768/1024) and fixed token_ids. All data is synthetic and public; no consumer data (A-001) is present. The patch excerpt shows vectors regenerated, e.g. adding additional_context enable_thinking=false to template_input, changing token counts and chain hashes. This looks like a template-rendering change for a Qwen-style model, and it changes expected cache keys and chain hashes. Security relevance is indirect: it touches the cross-tenant prefix-cache identity (T-041, TB-007). The fixture does not alter the scoped HMAC keys or at-rest encryption. Whether the provider's and any other consumer's implementation changes match these vectors, and whether the changed prompt_contract_id properly invalidates stale cache entries so a prior-contract artifact cannot be reused, lives in source files outside these units. I could not verify the corresponding Swift code, and the full patch is truncated, so only the fixture was examined. No concrete regression is identifiable from the fixture alone. Follow-up for integration: confirm that the code change behind these vector updates bumps the contract ID/cache key domain, and that enable_thinking=false cannot cause prompts with different semantics to share a chain hash.
